A single reference photograph of the small creature, cradled in two open gloved hands against a plain dark charcoal-grey background, lit with clean neutral studio light, flat and even, no environment, no props, no shadows cast on anything behind. The gloves are exactly those of the glove reference, worn on adult human hands, and they are the only thing visible besides the creature — no arm, no sleeve, no armour, no body, just the two gloved hands entering frame from below with their cuffs cut off by the bottom edge.
Size — the point of the sheet. The creature is exactly twice as large as it appears in the creature reference: double the length, double the height, double the bulk, the same animal grown to twice the size in every dimension. The gloved hands are the ruler and must read correctly. At this size it fills both cupped gloved hands completely, from the heel of the palms to the fingertips, with the head resting near the fingers and the hindquarters at the wrists. The fluid — it is soaking wet, not damp. Every square millimetre of the creature is coated in a clear, thick, viscous liquid. It is glazed head to foot in an unbroken film of it, so that no dry patch exists anywhere on its body — not on the top of its head, not on its back, not on the tips of its ears, not between its toes. Its down is plastered flat and dark against the skin in wet strands, swirls and spikes, revealing the shape of the skull and the ribs beneath. The liquid pools in every crease — the folds of the neck, the joints of the limbs, the hollow behind the ears — hangs in heavy stretched threads between its fingers and toes, gathers into a fat clear bead at the lowest point of its belly and at the tip of its tail, and runs down over the gloves: soaking the fingertips, filling the seams and panel lines of the gloves, pooling in the cupped palms beneath the body and making the whole surface of the gloves wet and shining. LOCATION SHEET — "THE RUN" — NANO BANANA
A photographed frame of the set, standing inside the burned library, dressed dense and lit like the film. Described from the top of the bay down to the floor. Salvaged instrument parts are buried in the wreck — the room can be played.

Prompt
A single photoreal cinematic film still, shot on 35mm, of one bay of shelving inside a burned library — the same library as the reference image, photographed in it. A thin dashed route with small numbered markers is laid lightly over the photograph. The picture underneath is a real frame from a film, not a drawing.
The reference image is the location and the look and must be matched exactly: the same architecture, scorched timber and shelf construction, the same swollen burnt books, the same ash and grime, the same haze, the same cold desaturated grey-green light, the same deep underexposed blacks, the same lens character and film grain. Take all the photography from it. Only the dressing of this one bay is designed.

THE FRAME — MANY SHELVES, REAL DEPTH
We are inside the library, standing back, slightly off square and a little low, seeing the shelving from ceiling to floor — and the route runs across several different bookcases, not one.
This is a corner of a room, built in depth like a 3D set, photographed with a real lens. There are at least four distinct runs of shelving in the picture, at different distances and different angles to us:
the near bay, closest to camera, its uprights cut by the left and right frame edges, sharp and detailed; a second unit standing at an angle to it, slightly further back and turned a few degrees, its boards catching the light along their front edges; a third run receding down an aisle into the dark, its shelves shortening away in perspective; a fourth, tipped and leaning against the others, half collapsed, wedged across the gap between two units.
They lean into each other and overlap. Boards from one unit have fallen across another; a plank spans from the near bay to the angled one; the gaps between units are as important as the units themselves. The route uses all of them — it crosses from shelving to shelving as it descends, passing from the near bay onto a fallen board bridging to the angled unit, back again, and down.
A heavy scorched timber column and the end of a fallen ceiling beam intrude at the top. The floor is covered edge to edge. Haze and slow dust fill the volume, thick enough to see the light moving through it and to separate each plane of shelving from the one behind it. Real depth: foreground detail sharp, the far aisle soft and swallowed by black.
The light: one weak, cold, grey-green source raking from high on one side, catching the top edges of the boards, the spines, the leaning planks and the brass — everything beneath falling to near-black. Deep shadow inside every shelf. No warm light, no fire, no amber, no glow, no visible lamp. Underexposed and pushed, coarse film grain, dirty milky shadows.

THE BAY, FROM THE TOP DOWN
Seven shelf levels at irregular heights, three metres tall, two metres wide. Scorched timber uprights either side, a broken central divider, black iron brackets — some bare, some still carrying boards, some hanging loose from one screw. Everything is filthy: char, water stain, swollen paper, grey dust.
THE ENTRY — the run comes from above, out of frame.
The route does not begin on the top board. It arrives there. From above the top of the picture, a long fallen plank angles down out of the darkness — from a higher bay or a collapsed upper shelf we never see — and lands on the top board, its lower end resting there. The dashed route runs down that plank from off the top edge of the frame, so the object is clearly coming from somewhere higher up, outside the shot. Above it, only black air, hanging paper and the underside of the fallen ceiling beam.
Above the top board. The bookcase's crown moulding is split and lifting. Wedged into the gap between the crown and the ceiling: a bundle of thin brass organ pipes, salvaged, of graded lengths, lying on their sides like a rack of tubes, blackened and dented, the longest as long as a forearm. Dust hangs off them. Cobweb and torn paper drape across the top.
LEVEL 7 — the top board. Swept clear along its length, pale where the dust has been disturbed. A crowd of upright scorched hardcovers presses in from the left end, spines swollen, gilt burned off. The right end is bare, its front lip intact and level. A single loose page lies half over the edge. Route point 01: the object stands here and runs right.
Between 7 and 6 — the first ramp. A fallen shelf board about a metre long leans from the right end of Level 7 down to the left onto Level 6, a shallow angle, its lower end resting on the board below, its upper end torn and splintered where it tore free. Its face is bare — a clean plank chute. Books are piled hard against both sides of it, holding it. Beneath it, in the shadow, a slack length of piano wire runs from a bracket to a nail, sagging. Route point 02.
LEVEL 6 — the book track. A continuous line of hardcovers laid flat, face down, all the same height, running the length of the board — a smooth lane. Behind the lane, upright books crowd shoulder to shoulder, one row collapsed into a slump. Set into the row, standing on end among the books, three short brass pipes of different lengths, upright like organ ranks, one leaning. At the right end of the lane, a black iron bracket stands proud of the board where the timber has burned away, a bent nail beside it, and just past the bracket the front lip is broken away in one clean bite. Route points 03 and 04.
Between 6 and 5 — the slot. Two leaning stacks of books form a narrow vertical channel, a hand's width wide, running down and slightly right, black inside. A thin brass tube is wedged vertically between the two stacks, running the depth of the slot — a chimney of dark metal with an object-sized bore. Route point 05.
LEVEL 5 — the sagging shelf. The board is cracked through the middle and sags, its right side dropped ten centimetres below its left, making a shallow chute. A slumped row of books leans along the back. Its front lip is split and folded downward at the right end. Nailed along the underside of this shelf, hanging free, a row of flat iron strips of graded lengths, like the bars of a broken glockenspiel, black with soot, one missing. Dust on their upper edges. Route point 06.
Across 5 and 4 — the ladder. A fallen wooden library ladder leans across two levels, old dark wood with iron fittings, rungs worn pale on their upper faces. The route runs a short distance along the flat top edge of one rung before dropping off the end. Books are piled through the ladder's frame. Route point 07.
Between 5 and 4 — the second ramp. A second fallen board leaning the opposite way, right down to left, steeper than the first, stacked books wedged beneath holding its angle. Bare face. Route point 08.
LEVEL 4 — the drawer. A cracked drawer pulled half out of its runner, its open top forming a short channel with two low sides, empty and swept. Around it: torn card indexes, a fan of loose pages, a book fallen open face down. Route point 09.
LEVEL 3 — the curve. A whole row of books has slumped sideways into a long shallow arc, their covers making a curved lane along the shelf. Behind them, upright volumes packed tight, and a small brass bell without a clapper lying on its side, dull and dented. Route point 10.
LEVEL 2 — the gap. The board is missing its centre section entirely — two broken, splintered ends and open black space between them. Books crowd both remaining ends, some tipped into the void. A single taut wire crosses the gap, strung from one broken end to the other, humming-tight. Route point 11.
LEVEL 1 — the last run. A short clear board, a single upright book standing at the far end like a marker, and past it the board simply stops: a clean overhang with nothing beneath it. The shelf that should sit below is gone — two bare black iron brackets on the uprights and open darkness under them. Route point 12.
BELOW — the drop. A metre of empty black air. In the shadow at the back of that space, barely legible, the frame of a small broken harp or piano soundboard leans against the boards, its remaining strings slack and dust-furred.
THE FLOOR. Bare scorched floorboards running toward the viewer. Swept clear in one lane directly beneath the overhang, running forward and out of the bottom of the frame. Everywhere else: drifted fallen books, splayed open volumes, loose pages, splintered board, ash, plaster dust. To one side, a card-catalogue cabinet with three drawers hanging open and cards spilled across the boards. A broken chair back. The lane itself is empty — nothing and no one stands in it. Route point 13.

THE BREAKAWAYS — LITTLE WOODS THAT SNAP
Thin wooden slats are set across the route, and they are made to break. Cheap scorched laths and thin dowels — the split backs of shelf boards, broken drawer sides, torn batten — spanning the path at four or five points, alternating from one side to the other so the route has to snap through them left, right, left, right as it descends.
Where they are: one thin lath bridging the top of the first plank chute, wedged between the board and the upright; a pair of narrow dowels crossing the mouth of the vertical slot, like bars over a gap; a splintered batten spanning the broken gap in the board, its two ends resting on the broken edges; a thin slat laid across the open front of the drawer; and a last frail lath across the very lip of the final overhang.
They are visibly weak — thin, dry, blackened, cracked along the grain, held by nothing but their own ends resting on something. They would not take any weight.
And two of them are already broken in this frame — snapped clean in the middle, the two halves hanging down from their ends, the fresh pale splintered break bright against the char, with a scatter of small pale splinters and wood dust on the board beneath. That fresh pale wood, in an otherwise entirely blackened room, is the one detail that tells you something has already come through here.
THE SUBTLE UNREAL
Everything above is a wreck. But the wreck is very slightly too musical, and very slightly too arranged. Keep this quiet — a viewer should feel it before noticing it:
the salvaged instrument parts — the graded brass pipes above the crown, the upright pipes among the books, the iron strips hanging like bars, the wires, the bell, the harp frame — are scattered as debris, not assembled, but they are always exactly where the route passes, as though the ruin had been tuned; the graded lengths repeat — pipes, iron strips and the fallen board lengths all step down in size in the same proportion, in three separate places; the spacing of the contact points is a little too even down the height of the bay, more regular than an accident would be; a few loose pages hang in the air, motionless, caught mid-fall, not blurred and not falling.
No glowing, no floating objects, no magic, no visible impossibility, no surreal distortion, no dreamlike softness. Everything obeys gravity and looks solid and photographed. The unreality is only in the arrangement, not in the physics.

THE PATH IS ONE CONTINUOUS LINE — BE EXACT
The dashed route is a single unbroken line from the top edge of the frame to the bottom edge of the frame. One line. It starts off the top of the picture, comes down the entry plank, travels through all thirteen contact points in order, drops through the last empty space, meets the floor, runs forward along the floor lane and exits off the bottom edge of the picture.
It never breaks, never stops, never has a gap, never restarts, never splits into branches, never forks, never loops, never crosses itself, never doubles back and never has arrows or separate segments. Every dash follows the one before it. From frame edge to frame edge, it is one continuous path.
Its shape: a descending zig-zag, alternating left and right on each level, each diagonal leg roughly the same length, with one straight vertical drop near the bottom where it falls through open air, and one straight horizontal run at the very end across the floor toward camera. The line is always in contact with a real surface in the picture except during that one vertical drop. It always sits on top of the boards, planks, book-lanes, the ladder rung and the drawer channel — never floating in space, never passing through wood, never running behind a shelf where it could not physically travel, and never taking a route the eye cannot follow.
The line must make sense as a physical path. Every diagonal follows the actual slope of a real leaning plank in the photograph. Every horizontal follows the actual top surface of a real board. If any part of the line does not lie on something solid, it is wrong.

The line above is drawn as a thin dashed white line, with a small thin circle at each contact point numbered 01 to 13 in small monospaced capitals. That is all. Delicate — never thick, never glowing, never dominating, never turning the image into a diagram.

AVOID
It is NOT a diagram, a blueprint, an orthographic elevation, a technical drawing, an exploded view, a museum display or a product shot. It is a photograph of a real place, with lens, depth, haze, grain and atmosphere. It has the geometry and completeness of a built 3D set, but the finish of a photographed one — never a clay render, never grey blockout, never untextured, never a game screenshot, never CGI-looking, never plastic, never over-clean: every surface is photoreal, textured, worn and filthy.
It is never a single flat shelving unit seen head-on. There must be several distinct runs of shelving at different depths and angles, overlapping and leaning into each other, with real perspective between them and haze separating the planes. If the picture is one shelf wall square to camera, it is wrong.
The bay is NEVER isolated on a flat background. No grey backdrop, no black void behind it, no floating unit, no studio surround, no drop shadow, no vignette frame, no empty margins. The library continues past all four edges. If the shelving is sitting alone on a flat field of colour, the image is wrong.
It is never sparse, clean, tidy or minimal. The bay is dense with books and wreckage, the floor is covered, the air is thick. An empty dark box with a few planks in it is wrong. If it looks calm, elegant or designed, it is wrong.
But the route stays clean — nothing sitting on the plank chutes, the flat-book lane, the ladder rung, the drawer channel or the last run, and nothing bridging the slot, the gap or the overhang. Complex everywhere, clear along the line.
No side-by-side detail insets, no thumbnail panels, no callout boxes, no leader lines, no arrows, no legend and no captions beyond the header, the thirteen numbers and the scale bar. One image, full frame.
No people anywhere — no figure, no legs, no boots, no feet, no hands, no face, no body, no silhouette.
No creature, no bird, no machine and no sphere in the set — the only sphere is the small one beside the scale bar, as a size reference.
The instrument parts are salvage, never a machine — no spiral tracks, no tubes assembled into a run, no rails, no funnels, no wheels, no gears, no pulleys, no keyboard, no complete instrument and nothing built for the purpose. Never a toy, a marble machine, a Rube Goldberg device, a music box or a game.
No colour except desaturated grey-green and the browns and blacks of scorched wood, paper and tarnished brass — no warm or golden grade, no amber, no orange, no firelight, no embers, no glow, no bloom, no flares, no neon, no coloured practicals, and no bright or polished brass — it is black, dull and dented. No clean or intact library, no polished wood, no bright books, no readable titles, no legible text on any spine. No fisheye, no barrel distortion, no wide-angle stretch. No watermark, no signature, no logo.

It is heavily blown out in the bright areas, where the green washes to near-white and detail is lost completely, and crushed to solid black in the shadows, with a wide soft band of mid-green haze between them. A very heavy vignette darkens all four corners and the whole frame bows outward with strong barrel distortion, as though seen through a cheap wide lens element pressed against glass — the horizontal lines curve, the top and bottom edges arc, and the corners stretch.
The image is dirty in every way an old sensor is dirty: fine horizontal scanlines running through the whole frame, a faint vertical weave texture over the left side, coarse luminance noise, blown highlight bloom smearing outward from the bright areas, dust and floating particles catching the light as thousands of tiny bright specks, and a shaft of falling debris coming down through the middle of the frame as a bright column of drifting motes. Along the left and right edges, faint vertical smears and dropouts. The picture looks recorded, degraded and re-photographed, not rendered.
Over the top of it sits a precise, tiny, clinical overlay drawn in thin crisp white one-pixel lines. Short white measurement bars — flat dashes of varying length — clustered around the centre of interest, some paired above and below like a crop indicator, some standing vertically. A small cluster of narrow stepped bar graphs low in the bottom left corner with tiny digits beside them. A tiny percentage mark and a stack of digits down the far left edge.

There is no photograph, no room, no environment and no scene behind the graphics — the background is solid black from edge to edge, and everything in the image is screen graphics floating on that black.
Palette. Everything is drawn in a narrow range of electric cyan and pale teal, with a few small readouts in a dim sickly green, and nothing else. No white, no red, no orange, no yellow, no purple. The lines are thin, crisp and vector-sharp, glowing very slightly against the black with a faint phosphor bloom, never thick and never neon-bright.
Centre. In the middle of the frame, a circular scan window about half the height of the picture. Inside it, and only inside it, sits the one photographic element in the whole image: a soft, abstract, out-of-focus thermal reading of a human head and shoulders, rendered in blotchy blue, cyan and acid green, smeared and stretched by motion into curved streaks, unreadable as a face and readable as a living body — hot pale patches, cold dark voids, banding and vertical smear through the lower third. It is heavily blurred and confined strictly inside the circle. It has no hard edge against the black: it fades out at the circle's boundary. A tiny cyan crosshair sits at its centre.
Dials. Around the scan window, two concentric circular structures. The outer one is a very large ring of hundreds of fine radial tick marks — a dense dashed dial spanning almost the full height of the frame, brightest at the sides and fading toward the top and bottom. Inside it, two thin arc segments, upper and lower, in a dimmer grey-cyan, not closing into a full circle.
Left column. A vertical numeric scale running down the left side, in small cyan monospaced digits, reading from the top: 260.0, 240.0, 220.0, 200.0, 180.0, 120.0, 100.0, 80.0, 60.0, 40.0, 20.0. Two short horizontal indicator rules extend to the right from this scale toward the dial — one dim green at the 260.0 line, one pale at the 180.0 line.
Right panels. Three stacked data blocks against the right edge, each identical in construction. Each has two solid filled cyan rectangles containing large dark numerals, one above the other, with a unit abbreviation beside each. Beneath each pair, four lines of very small text, and a min/max row. The blocks read, top to bottom: H R — 38 BPM and 38 BPM, with MIN 25 MAX 180 broken across stacked characters; PRESSURE, its letters set vertically one per line down the left of the block — 12 P and 12 P, with MIN 10 MAX 50; TWITCH, also set vertically — 3/1 T/S and 3/1 T/S, with MIN 1/1 MAX 10/1. The filled boxes are the brightest things in the whole image.
Upper readouts. Two identical rows of small cyan telemetry across the upper middle, above the scan window, each reading 236 Ms at the left and 932 hPa at the right, generously spaced.
Lower readouts. Beneath the scan window, a horizontal axis marked 0.0, 0.20, 0.40, 1.00 at wide intervals. Below it, two rows of small figures: 0.1 A with 0324 mAh, and 0.8 A with 1784 mAh. Lower still, a faint row of dim digits.
Corners. Bottom left, small cyan monospaced text reading M VARI - 02 with a small hollow circle beside it. Bottom right, two stacked lines reading M VARI - 02 and M VARI - 03, with two small empty squares to their left. Thin faint rules divide the top and bottom margins of the frame from the centre.
Top left — the brand. In the top left corner, the YGGD logo from the attached reference, redrawn large and clean as a thin hollow cyan outline — glyphs made of open strokes, not filled shapes, in the manner of an engraved plate or an outline typeface. It sits at the top of a three-line header block; beneath it, in much smaller cyan monospaced capitals, two lines reading BASELINE TEST and 1.3.6.1. Finish. The whole plate is a screen, and looks photographed off one: very faint horizontal scanlines, gentle phosphor bloom around the brightest strokes, a soft dark falloff toward the corners, and slight chromatic softness at the edges of the glowing lines. Cinematic, restrained, the aesthetic of a near-future forensic diagnostic display in a science fiction film.
Avoid. No background image of any kind — no room, no library, no landscape, no texture, no gradient sky, no photographic plate behind the graphics. Solid black everywhere the graphics are not. The only photographic content is inside the central circle. No white, red, orange, yellow or purple anywhere. No rotating 3D wireframes, no hexagons, no honeycomb, no polygon meshes, no glowing icons, no progress bars filling, no fingerprint or DNA helix motifs, no world maps. The YGGD logo appears once only, in the top left, as a hollow cyan outline — never filled, never coloured, never on a badge or plate, never repeated, never centred. Reference. The attached image supplies only the machine's materials, its surface finish, its panel-line language and its grime — matte grey armour, fine seams, worn edges. Its silhouette is not preserved. In this sheet the machine has reconfigured and no longer looks like a bird in any way.

A prop and VFX reference sheet for a small piece of ordnance, laid out flat on an even dark charcoal-grey background. Landscape, 16:9, clean technical presentation, neutral studio lighting, no environment, no floor plane, no shadows cast.
The object. The bird machine has folded itself shut into a dense armoured seed. Its wings have wrapped forward and locked around the body; its legs have drawn up and inverted; its head has retracted entirely into the mass. What remains is a single compact form roughly 15 centimetres long: a heavy tapered ovoid, wide and blunt at the crown and drawn to a point at the base, its surface built from tightly overlapping armour scales that spiral around the body like the scales of a pine cone or the husk of a beech nut. The plates are matte grey, worn at their edges, industrially machined, with fine grime in every seam — the same material and wear as the reference. It reads as engineered, agricultural and cruel: a metal seed, made to be planted.
Its armed state. Between every overlapping scale, a continuous hairline of hard saturated red glows out from inside, brightest at the spiralling seams around the widest part of the body and fading toward the crown. At the crown, where the head went in, a single dark circular aperture with a red iris burning deep inside it. Set flush into one flank, a small rectangular display showing hard white seven-segment numerals with a decimal, reading tenths and hundredths. Around the base, three short claw-shaped anchors have driven out of the shell and splayed wide, locking the object down onto whatever it is standing on, their tips bitten in. No fins, no nose cone, no fuse, no wick, no warhead shape.
Layout. Across the top of the sheet, a small transformation strip of three silhouettes in sequence, drawn smaller than the main views: the original bird machine standing, then a mid-fold state with the plating rotating and wrapping and the legs inverting, then the sealed seed. Beneath it, four large views of the sealed armed object, all lit identically: side elevation at the left, three-quarter front in the centre, top-down at the upper right showing the spiral of the scales converging on the crown aperture, and base-up at the lower right showing the three splayed anchors.
Annotation. Thin white one-pixel leader lines with small right-angle elbows point to details, labelled in tiny monospaced type: the crown aperture, the seam glow, the flank counter, the anchor claws, the scale overlap. Along the bottom, a plain scale bar marked 15 cm with a small human hand silhouette beside it for comparison. Small monospaced header text at the top left reading BRD-1 // ORDNANCE FORM.
Finish. Photographic material rendering — machined matte metal, fine grime, worn edges, subtle specular on the scale edges. The register of a real film production's prop reference sheet. Precise, filmic, restrained.
Avoid. No bird. No wings, no beak, no head, no tail, no feathers, no legs, no bird silhouette anywhere in the four main views — only the transformation strip may show the bird, and only in its first frame. No classic bomb clichés: no round black cartoon bomb, no burning fuse, no dynamite sticks, no ticking alarm clock, no missile, no artillery shell, no fins, no nose cone, no warhead. No environment, background scenery, smoke, fire, explosion, sparks or motion blur. Nothing is cracked, burned or blown apart — this is armed, not destroyed. No blue, orange or green glow: the only emissive colour is the hard red, plus the white of the numerals. No text other than the labels described. Never larger than 15 centimetres.

# NANO BANANA — SKY REPLACEMENT — THE ANCHOR IN THE PIT

<<<image_1>>> — THE PLATE, AND THE SOLE EDITING MASTER. The low upward angle from inside the pit: rubble edges framing the bottom and both sides, rusted rebar entering at upper right, the YGGD anchor device seated on the rock at bottom centre with its steel cable running off to the right, a small dark bird high in the sky, and a bright sky crossed by strong fanned shafts of sunlight.

【THIS EDIT CHANGES THE SKY AND NOTHING ELSE.】

---

## THE CHANGE — A HEAVY OVERCAST SKY

【REPLACE THE ENTIRE VISIBLE SKY WITH FULL, HEAVY, OVERCAST CLOUD.】 Layered grey stratus and broken altocumulus filling every part of the sky, with real depth and structure: darker slate-grey masses lower down, paler cooler grey higher up, soft torn edges where one layer passes in front of another, subtle internal shading giving the cloud volume rather than a flat painted texture.

【COMPLETELY COVERED — no blue, no clear patches, no gaps of open sky, no bright horizon band.】 A solid, brooding, weather-heavy overcast.

## THE SUN RAYS ARE REMOVED — THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PART

【EVERY ONE OF THE FANNED SHAFTS OF LIGHT IN <<<image_1>>> IS GONE.】 No god rays, no crepuscular rays, no beams, no shafts, no bright hotspot where the sun was, no glowing patch behind the cloud, no silver-lined cloud edge, no lens flare, no glare, no halo.

【THE SKY IS EVENLY DULL AND DIFFUSE — NOTHING IN IT INDICATES WHERE THE SUN IS. If a viewer could point at the sun's position, the edit has failed.】

The bright blown-out area at the top of frame where the sun sat is replaced by ordinary cloud at the same brightness as the rest of the sky — 【NO RESIDUAL BRIGHT PATCH, NO LINGERING GLOW, NO FAINT GHOST OF THE OLD RAYS.】

FAIL: any ray, beam, shaft or god ray survives or is re-drawn = SHOT FAILED. FAIL: a bright disc, hotspot or glowing area marking the sun = SHOT FAILED. FAIL: a silver-lined or backlit cloud edge = wrong. FAIL: any flare, bloom, glare or halo = wrong. FAIL: warm, golden, orange or pink tones anywhere = wrong, it is cold and grey.

## THE LIGHT MUST NOW AGREE WITH THE NEW SKY

【THE ROCK, THE REBAR AND THE ANCHOR DEVICE WERE LIT BY HARD DIRECTIONAL SUN. UNDER A HEAVY OVERCAST THEY WOULD NOT BE.】 Soften the light on them to match the new sky: reduce the hard highlights and the bright rim along the top edges of the rubble and the anchor's upper casing, open up and soften the shadows so nothing reads as a sharp cast shadow, and let everything sit in flat, even, shadowless light.

【KEEP THIS SUBTLE AND KEEP EVERY OBJECT ITSELF UNCHANGED — this is a lighting adjustment on the existing objects, not a redesign of them. Do not move, reshape, replace or re-texture anything.】

FAIL: hard directional highlights or sharp cast shadows remain while the sky is overcast = wrong, the light must agree with the sky. FAIL: the foreground is re-lit so heavily that objects change shape, colour or material = wrong.

Untouched, pixel for pixel in position and form:

**THE ANCHOR DEVICE** — its shape, its dirty off-white casing, the red YGGD tree mark, the printed lettering, the ribbed band, the dark upper cap, the orange collar at its base, and every scuff and stain on it. 【DO NOT REDRAW, RE-LABEL OR CLEAN UP ANY OF ITS MARKINGS.】

**THE STEEL CABLE** — same curve, same slack, same position running off to the right, same braided texture.

**THE RUBBLE AND ROCK** — every stone, crack and edge exactly where it is, including the soft out-of-focus masses at the left and right edges. 【THE SILHOUETTE OF THE ROCK AGAINST THE SKY IS EXACT — the cloud stops precisely at that edge with no bleeding, no glow spilling onto the stone, no halo, no softening or re-drawing of the rock line.】

**THE REBAR AT UPPER RIGHT** — its exact position, thickness, rusted texture and out-of-focus rendering. 【CLOUD APPEARS BEHIND IT, NEVER OVER IT, and its edges are not thickened, blurred further or lost into the sky.】

**THE BIRD** — 【THE SMALL DARK BIRD HIGH IN THE SKY STAYS, in its exact position, at its exact size and shape. It now reads as a dark silhouette against cloud instead of against bright sky.】 It is not removed, moved, enlarged or duplicated.

**THE FRAMING** — identical crop, identical composition, identical aspect ratio. Nothing is added at the edges.

Monumental history painting of a bullring at the moment after the kill — three elements only. The black bull lies dead on its side in the raked sand, a dozen banderillas bristling upright from its shredded shoulders, ribbons soaked black-red and dripping, a sword buried to the hilt between the withers. Blood is everywhere on the animal: pouring in a thick unbroken rope from its open mouth, running from both nostrils, sheeting down the barrel of its body from every barb wound, matting the hide into wet clotted ridges, pooling in the folds of its neck. Beneath and around it a vast lake of blood has spread across the sand — metres wide, deep enough to hold a mirror reflection of the torero standing in it, its edge creeping outward in dark fingers where the sand drinks it, its centre still liquid and glossy, skinned over and rippling faintly, with long drag-streaks and hoof-scuffs printed through it. The torero stands alone at the edge of that pool, boots stained to the ankle, in his gold-embroidered traje de luces, montera in hand, turned toward the stands. Behind them the tiered ranks of the audience rise in their thousands behind the barrera, under a colonnaded gallery. Nothing else in the arena — no horses, no attendants, no mules, the sand beyond the blood completely empty.
Lit by one narrow shaft of hard light falling from high and far to the left, striking only the torero, the dead bull and the pool of blood, holding them in a tight island of illumination and nothing more. Inside that shaft the light is fierce and near-white — blazing on the gold bullion of the jacket until it burns out to pure lead white, raking across the wet black hide so it reads like oiled stone, and igniting the blood into a sheet of molten crimson that becomes the brightest colour in the painting, throwing warm red bounce up onto the man's jaw and hands from below. Outside it, everything collapses. The fall-off is violent, one hand's breadth from lit to unreadable: the sand goes bone white to umber to black within a metre of the pool's edge, the barrera is barely a suggestion, and the entire audience — all thousands of them — is swallowed into dense warm blackness, present only as the faintest scatter of pale smudges where a brow or a collar catches a stray photon, more felt than seen. The colonnaded gallery above is absolute black. Ninety percent of the canvas is shadow, transparent and glazed rather than flat, so the darkness has depth and heat in it. No fill light anywhere. No sky. Spotlight-hard, altar-like, the bodies and the blood burning out of an ocean of dark.
Zurbarán, Seville c.1640. The same darkness turned mystical and utterly silent. Everything stills: the torero stands motionless and frontal like a saint in a devotional panel, sculpturally simplified, the folds of his cape rendered with hard clean edges and a chalky matte white that seems lit from within. The blood pool is a single perfect black-crimson shape, almost geometric. Ascetic, hushed, no motion, no gesture, no crowd noise — the arena as chapel and the animal as offering. Reverent rather than gruesome.
Composed at grand-manner scale — three metres across, figures near life-size, deep recession into darkness, a governing diagonal running from the carcass up to the invisible gallery. Oil on linen, generations of ambered varnish, fine age craquelure across the darks, faint stretcher-bar lines. Photographed straight-on in a museum gallery, heavy carved and gilded frame at the edges, the surface reading as enormous.

Monumental history painting of a bullring at the moment after the kill — three elements only. The black bull lies dead on its side in the raked sand, a dozen banderillas bristling upright from its shredded shoulders, ribbons soaked black-red and dripping, a sword buried to the hilt between the withers. Blood is everywhere on the animal: pouring in a thick unbroken rope from its open mouth, running from both nostrils, sheeting down the barrel of its body from every barb wound, matting the hide into wet clotted ridges, pooling in the folds of its neck. Beneath and around it a vast lake of blood has spread across the sand — metres wide, deep enough to hold a mirror reflection of the torero standing in it, its edge creeping outward in dark fingers where the sand drinks it, its centre still liquid and glossy, skinned over and rippling faintly, with long drag-streaks and hoof-scuffs printed through it. The torero stands alone at the edge of that pool, boots stained to the ankle, in his gold-embroidered traje de luces, montera in hand, turned toward the stands. Behind them the tiered ranks of the audience rise in their thousands behind the barrera, under a colonnaded gallery. Nothing else in the arena — no horses, no attendants, no mules, the sand beyond the blood completely empty.
Lit by one narrow shaft of hard light falling from high and far to the left, striking only the torero, the dead bull and the pool of blood, holding them in a tight island of illumination and nothing more. Inside that shaft the light is fierce and near-white — blazing on the gold bullion of the jacket until it burns out to pure lead white, raking across the wet black hide so it reads like oiled stone, and igniting the blood into a sheet of molten crimson that becomes the brightest colour in the painting, throwing warm red bounce up onto the man's jaw and hands from below. Outside it, everything collapses. The fall-off is violent, one hand's breadth from lit to unreadable: the sand goes bone white to umber to black within a metre of the pool's edge, the barrera is barely a suggestion, and the entire audience — all thousands of them — is swallowed into dense warm blackness, present only as the faintest scatter of pale smudges where a brow or a collar catches a stray photon, more felt than seen. The colonnaded gallery above is absolute black. Ninety percent of the canvas is shadow, transparent and glazed rather than flat, so the darkness has depth and heat in it. No fill light anywhere. No sky. Spotlight-hard, altar-like, the bodies and the blood burning out of an ocean of dark.
Goya, Madrid c.1820. The black manner. Ugly, fast, savagely economical — pigment scrubbed on thin with rags and stiff brushes, forms half-dissolved, anatomy summary and wrong in ways that make it worse. The light dirty rather than divine, a sick greenish white. The audience out of the dark becomes a mass of leering half-formed faces, and the torero is small, mean and ordinary against the enormous dead animal. Bone black, dirty ochre, a filthy carmine. No nobility anywhere. Modern in its bleakness, painted like a witness rather than an artist.
Composed at grand-manner scale — three metres across, figures near life-size, deep recession into darkness, a governing diagonal running from the carcass up to the invisible gallery. Oil on linen, generations of ambered varnish, fine age craquelure across the darks, faint stretcher-bar lines. Photographed straight-on in a museum gallery, heavy carved and gilded frame at the edges, the surface reading as enormous.

NO REFERENCE IMAGES. EVERYTHING IS DESCRIBED IN WORDS BELOW.

TWO THINGS FIRST
【NOTHING GOES IN HIS EYES. The irises are clean and empty — no tree, no symbol, no logo, no reflection, no image, no glow, nothing composited or floating in them. Only ordinary catchlights.】
【HIS FACE IS CLEAN. No blood, no dirt, no dust, no grime, no smears, no cuts, no wounds, no bruises, no swelling, no sweat. He has not been hurt and he has not been anywhere. His skin is simply his own skin.】
FAIL: anything at all placed inside an iris = shot failed. FAIL: blood, dirt or injuries anywhere on his face = shot failed.

WHO HE IS — BUILD THIS FACE
A TEENAGE BOY, sixteen or seventeen years old. 【HE MUST READ AS A CHILD, NOT AS A YOUNG MAN.】
Slight build, narrow shoulders, a long thin neck. Head shaved down to a few millimetres of dark stubble, with the hairline still readable as a slightly darker line across the forehead and around the ears. Pale skin.
Heavy, dark, straight eyebrows sitting low over the eyes. Wide-set eyes, large, pale green-grey, with long dark lashes. A straight small nose, slightly upturned at the tip. A soft full mouth, relaxed and unset. A round chin and a jaw that has not hardened yet. Ears standing a little proud of the skull, the rims translucent pink where light passes through them.
【THE SKIN IS HONEST AND UNRETOUCHED.】 A scatter of small freckles across the bridge of the nose and the upper cheeks. Faint teenage blemishes and small red spots on the cheeks and the chin. Uneven tone, a flush across the cheekbones and the tops of the ears. Visible pores. Fine downy hair at the temples. Dry, slightly chapped lips. Thin shadows under the eyes.
ONE OLD SCAR. A short pale healed line, about two centimetres, crossing his LEFT EYEBROW — his own left, which appears on the RIGHT-HAND SIDE of the picture when he faces camera. It breaks the eyebrow hair in a small gap. It is old, flat and pale. Only one, and nowhere else on his face.
FAIL: an adult, a young man, a soldier or a hardened face = shot failed. FAIL: airbrushed, poreless, symmetrical or model-perfect skin = shot failed. FAIL: a beard, moustache, long hair or any hair beyond the shaved stubble = wrong. FAIL: extra scars, cuts, blood, bruises, dirt, dust or grime on the face = shot failed. HE IS COMPLETELY CLEAN AND UNINJURED.
WHAT HE IS WEARING — BUILD THIS ARMOUR
A hard-shell articulated exosuit worn over a dark undersuit.
DIRTY BONE-WHITE AND PALE GREY composite plating, matte, never glossy, never chrome. MUTED BRICK-RED accent panels on the shoulders and upper arms. BLACK rubberised joints at the shoulders and elbows. Fine engraved panel lines and small recessed fasteners across every plate.
A RAISED WHITE COLLAR RING stands up around his throat like a padded gorget — thick, scuffed, dirty along its top edge.
ON THE UPPER CHEST, BELOW THE COLLAR: A SMALL RED EMBLEM — a simple stylised tree glyph, a vertical stem with branches spreading upward and roots angling down, printed flat in a single desaturated red. Under it, one line of tiny stencilled capitals, worn and only half legible.
Pale grey dust worked into every seam, panel line and recess. It is worn equipment, not new gear.
FAIL: glossy, chrome, brand-new or superhero armour = wrong, it is dirty worn kit. FAIL: glowing panels, lights, screens or LEDs anywhere = shot failed. FAIL: a helmet, visor or face covering = wrong, his head is bare. FAIL: weapons, guns or gear in frame = wrong.
THE IDEA — HE IS A BOY IN A WAR SUIT
【THE ARMOUR IS HARD AND INDUSTRIAL. THE FACE INSIDE IT IS SOFT, YOUNG AND COMPLETELY UNPROTECTED. THAT CONTRADICTION IS THE POSTER.】
He should read as someone far too young to be wearing this. The suit is equipment; the face is a person.
FAIL: he looks like a hero, a badass or a veteran = shot failed. FAIL: a determined jaw, a squint, a scowl, a smirk = wrong. FAIL: an action pose, a gesture, a weapon = wrong.

THE MEDIUM — THIS ONE IS DRAWN, NOT PHOTOGRAPHED
【A HAND-PAINTED CEL-ANIMATION ILLUSTRATION IN THE LATE-EIGHTIES / EARLY-NINETIES JAPANESE ANIMATED FILM IDIOM.】 Airbrushed gouache and cel paint over a painted background — not digital, not 3D, not photographic, not a photo with a filter.
Crisp inked outlines of varying weight around the figure and the armour. Flat colour fields with HARD-EDGED shadow shapes — a clean line where light stops and shadow begins, no soft gradients on the skin. Specular highlights painted as solid shapes. Subtle cel and paper texture, slight registration imperfection, visible brushwork in the background.
【THE STYLISATION NEVER OVERRIDES THE FACE DESCRIBED ABOVE. His eyes stay realistically proportioned — not enlarged, not anime-huge, not glassy — with painted irises and a hard-edged catchlight.】
THE COMPOSITION
Vertical poster format. A three-quarter head-and-shoulders portrait, the head large and slightly above centre, chin a fraction down, eyes to the viewer. The collar ring and both shoulder plates fill the lower corners; the chest emblem painted crisply below the collar. The armour rendered with hard mechanical precision — every panel line a deliberate painted shape — against the softness of the face.
Behind him: a deep dark field, almost black, with one broad diffuse shaft of pale light falling from an upper corner and fine painted dust motes drifting in it. Nothing readable — no city, no machinery, no location.
Painted with a soft warm key from the front so his face is the warmest thing in the picture.
FAIL: photorealism or a photo run through a filter = shot failed. FAIL: 3D render, CGI, plastic shading = wrong. FAIL: modern flat vector or thin-line webcomic style = wrong. FAIL: speed lines, explosions, energy effects = wrong. FAIL: any Japanese lettering, kanji or katakana = shot failed.

THE EYES
Large in frame, wet and catching the light, faintly reddened at the rims, with clear catchlights. Every eyelash separated. The irises rendered in full — fibres, striations, the dark limbal ring, the pupil.
He looks straight out at the viewer. 【OPEN AND UNGUARDED. NOT FIERCE, NOT BLANK, NOT SAD, NOT PLEADING — JUST PRESENT, AND SLIGHTLY MORE VULNERABLE THAN HE WOULD LIKE TO BE.】 The eyes are wet, but there are no tears on his face.

a crowded stone bullring seen from a high box — the black bull lies dead on its side in the raked sand, a dozen banderillas bristling upright from its shredded shoulders, ribbons of red and yellow soaked dark, a sword buried to the hilt between the withers, blood running thick from its mouth and nostrils into a wide glistening pool that spreads across the pale sand and streaks where the body was dragged. Beside it the picador's disembowelled horse lies twisted in its torn caparison. A mozo in blue stands over the carcass with a short blade; the tiered crowd rises behind the barrera under a colonnaded gallery, one crimson cloth hung over the balustrade.

Spanish Golden Age Baroque, c.1640. Sober silver-grey light, restrained earth palette of black, bone white, ochre and oxblood, immense dignity in the standing figures, dead flesh painted with cold anatomical honesty, backgrounds thin and atmospheric. Fluid loaded brush, nothing overworked.

Venetian Baroque tenebrism, c.1620. One hard shaft of light falling across the opened body while the rest of the arena drowns in warm near-black, the wounds modelled in glazed crimson lake and brown, wet viscera catching a single white highlight, gold thread glinting on the mozo's sleeve. Thick lead-white impasto in the lit passages, transparent brown darks, butchery painted like a martyrdom.

A high-angle wide shot captures a busy, sunlit bullring, densely crowded with spectators on tiered stone benches shaded beneath a colonnaded gallery. In the raked ochre sand, a striking tableau unfolds: a large, muscular black bull built from writhing dark strokes lowers its head and charges, its withers bristling with banderillas striped in red and yellow. A picador's armored, blindfolded horse, rendered in thick, grayish pigment, buckles under the assault while a vibrant blue-clad mozo strains at the reins. One crimson cloth is draped boldly over the foreground balustrade. Every surface glistens with heavy-handed impasto, lent a sculptural quality by swirling ribbons and peaks of oil paint, creating a tactile sense of light and atmosphere. The sun rakes across the arena, casting hard-edged shadows in chromatic blues, contrasting ochre highlights and cobalt shadows, while the sky twists above in turbulent indigo and turquoise vortexes. Colors clash in saturated, primary hues with complementary accents, typical of c.1889 French Post-Impressionism. The overall composition is tightly packed, dynamic, and emotionally charged, with the sense of crowd, action, and heat heightened by texture and painterly, grainy surface details approximating an analog film look. The scene is vivid, lively, and tense, evoking the raw physicality, chaos, and ritualism of the bullfight with tactile intensity.

A wide, high-angle shot presents a crowded stone bullring as painted in a c.1815 Spanish Romantic oil artwork, the scene viewed from the perspective of a box. The foreground centers on a black bull, definitively dead and sprawled on its side, glazed dark blood pooling from its mouth and nostrils, streaking the raked pale ochre sand. Vividly colored ribbons—reds and yellows—drip from over a dozen banderillas fixed to its shredded, bloodied shoulders, while a sword is visible thrust down to the hilt between its withers. Adjacent, a twisted carcass of a horse in a torn, colored caparison is displayed, disemboweled and gory, with a standing mozo in a blue outfit overseeing the scene, holding a short blade. The midground and background are dominated by a tiered, densely packed crowd represented by thousands of loose pink, gray, and ivory paint dabs, filling stands behind the barrera under a colonnaded gallery. A single vivid crimson cloth hangs over the balustrade. The lighting is bright and diffuse, sending chalky, sun-soaked highlights across the sand contrasted against transparent shadow. The overall color palette juxtaposes pale sandy ochre, deep madder red, dark bull, and lively crowd tints, with warm umber underpainting showing through. The visible canvas weave, widespread craquelure, and aged glossy varnish suggest this is a museum-quality photograph of an antique oil painting. Acutely high in visual drama and painterly fragmentation, the scene is cinematic, gory, and unsettlingly grand, evoking a sense of spectacle and tragedy.

## WHAT IT IS

A HAND-SIZED DESCENT ANCHOR from a used, field-worn science-fiction infantry kit. A tool, not sports gear: you press it against stone, it bites in, and you go down the line.

【MINIMAL. FEW PARTS. FEW SEAMS. NOTHING FUSSY.】 The design language is quiet and industrial — smooth machined volumes, one or two clean shut-lines, chamfered edges, no clutter. NO exposed wiring, NO greebles, NO rivets everywhere, NO pipes, NO glowing screens, NO holographic displays, NO buttons scattered over it, NO decorative panelling. It is a solid object that looks milled from a single billet.

**THE BODY.** A flattened rounded-rectangular puck, roughly the size of a palm and about three centimetres thick — a shape that sits comfortably in a gloved hand. DIRTY BONE-WHITE composite shell over a GUNMETAL alloy core, the two materials meeting on one crisp shut-line around the perimeter. Matte throughout. Machined tool finish. Never chrome, never glossy, never new.

**THE ANCHORING FACE.** The underside is the business end: a recessed flat contact plate of dark grey alloy, and set into it THREE SHORT, THICK, TAPERED SPIKES arranged in a triangle, currently DRIVEN OUT and standing proud by about four centimetres. They are hardened dark steel, faceted, blunt-tipped, and BADLY WORN — bright scratched metal showing through at the tips, pale stone dust and grey grit packed into their bases and into the recess around them. This device has been punched into a lot of walls.

**THE CORD.** A single GREY STEEL CABLE, THIN — only three or four millimetres — feeding out of a narrow slot in one end of the body. Fine multi-strand wire rope: a tight helical lay of many hair-thin steel filaments, cool neutral grey, with a low satin sheen that catches the light in a broken line along its length rather than as one clean highlight. Dry, dusty, faintly darkened with handling, one or two filaments sprung proud where it has been abused. A short length of it lies out of the device in one long relaxed S-curve across the surface, holding a slight springy memory in the bend, ending in a swaged dark alloy ferrule.

【IT IS A THIN STEEL CABLE, NOT A ROPE】 Not thick, not fluffy, not fibrous, not woven textile, not a coil of mountaineering rope, not golden, not white. FAIL TEST: IF IT LOOKS LIKE ORDINARY ROPE OR TEXTILE CORD, IT IS WRONG.

**THE CONTROLS.** Exactly two, and no more: a single low-profile knurled brake wheel set flush into one long edge, and one small recessed trigger stud beside it. Nothing else. No display, no lights, no labels beyond the mark below.

**THE ORANGE.** SAFETY ORANGE is the device's one accent colour, and it is used sparingly and functionally, exactly where a tool would carry it: the KNURLED BRAKE WHEEL is anodised orange, rubbed back to raw metal on its high points; the RECESSED TRIGGER STUD is orange; and a single THIN ORANGE LINE is inset into the shut-line running around the perimeter of the body, broken and worn away in places. Matte, dusty, scuffed — a hard anodised industrial orange, NOT bright, NOT plastic, NOT glowing, NOT neon. It covers only a small fraction of the object. PROP SHEET — THE DESCENT ANCHOR — YGGD — NANO BANANA
A clean PROP REFERENCE PLATE of a single piece of equipment: a compact descent device with an aramid line. This is a still image of one object, not a scene.
WHAT IT IS
A HAND-SIZED DESCENT ANCHOR from a used, field-worn science-fiction infantry kit. A tool, not sports gear: you press it against stone, it bites in, and you go down the line.
【MINIMAL. FEW PARTS. FEW SEAMS. NOTHING FUSSY.】 The design language is quiet and industrial — smooth machined volumes, one or two clean shut-lines, chamfered edges, no clutter. NO exposed wiring, NO greebles, NO rivets everywhere, NO pipes, NO glowing screens, NO holographic displays, NO buttons scattered over it, NO decorative panelling. It is a solid object that looks milled from a single billet.
THE BODY. A flattened rounded-rectangular puck, roughly the size of a palm and about three centimetres thick — a shape that sits comfortably in a gloved hand. DIRTY BONE-WHITE composite shell over a GUNMETAL alloy core, the two materials meeting on one crisp shut-line around the perimeter. Matte throughout. Machined tool finish. Never chrome, never glossy, never new.
THE ANCHORING FACE. The underside is the business end: a recessed flat contact plate of dark grey alloy, and set into it THREE SHORT, THICK, TAPERED SPIKES arranged in a triangle, currently DRIVEN OUT and standing proud by about four centimetres. They are hardened dark steel, faceted, blunt-tipped, and BADLY WORN — bright scratched metal showing through at the tips, pale stone dust and grey grit packed into their bases and into the recess around them. This device has been punched into a lot of walls.
THE LINE. A single strand of ARAMID / KEVLAR cord, THIN — only four or five millimetres — feeding out of a narrow slot in one end of the body. It is DULL GOLDEN-TAN, the unmistakable colour of raw aramid, tightly braided with a fine visible weave, dusty and slightly fuzzed with use, matte and dry-looking. A short length of it lies out of the device in one long relaxed S-curve across the surface, ending in a heat-sealed dark alloy ferrule.
【THE LINE IS THIN AND TECHNICAL, NOT A CLIMBING ROPE】 It is not thick, not fluffy, not a coil of mountaineering rope, not white, not braided nylon. FAIL TEST: IF IT LOOKS LIKE ORDINARY ROPE, IT IS WRONG.
THE CONTROLS. Exactly two, and no more: a single low-profile knurled brake wheel set flush into one long edge, and one small recessed trigger stud beside it. Nothing else. No display, no lights, no labels beyond the marking below.
LOGO LAW
YGGD is laser-etched into the flat top face of the body, small, off to one side rather than centred — set in a condensed, squared, industrial sans-serif and filled with MUTED BRICK RED, half rubbed away by wear. Beneath it, in much smaller dark grey stencil characters, a short serial and a load rating — legible as marks, not necessarily as words.
【THE WORD IS Y-G-G-D. FOUR LETTERS. NOTHING ELSE.】
Spelled correctly, appearing exactly once. NO tagline, NO second brand, NO invented lettering, NO script, NO glow, NO emblem, NO circle around it, NO barcode. Industrial stamping, not a fashion label.
FAIL TEST: IF THE LETTERS ARE MISSPELLED, DUPLICATED, REVERSED OR JOINED INTO NONSENSE, IT IS WRONG.
PHOTOGRAPHY
Shot on 35mm anamorphic — oval bokeh in any out-of-focus highlight, horizontal smear on speculars, a touch of barrel distortion, corners softer than centre, fine film grain in the shadows.
THREE-QUARTER HIGH ANGLE looking down onto the device where it rests on a flat surface, tipped slightly so that BOTH the top face with the marking AND the spiked underside are readable at once. The whole object sits inside the frame with clean air around it — nothing cropped, nothing crowded.
SURFACE AND BACKGROUND
A plain, flat, seamless studio surface in NEUTRAL MID-GREY, falling off softly to darker grey at the edges. NO table edge, NO wood grain, NO concrete texture, NO fabric, NO props, NO tools, NO hands, NO people, NO location, NO horizon, NO text overlay, NO watermark, NO measurement scale, NO callout lines or arrows, NO multi-view turnaround panels, NO exploded diagram.
【ONE OBJECT, ONE FRAME, NOTHING ELSE IN THE PICTURE】
LIGHT
One large soft key from high and slightly to one side, raking across the body so the machined edges, the shut-line, the knurling and the weave of the aramid read in relief, with a soft shadow falling away. A weak cool fill opposite so the shadow side is dark but not black. Hard small speculars on the alloy and on the spike tips, none blown out. NOTHING glows. NO practical light, NO lens flare, NO rim halo, NO coloured gels.
COLOUR
Desaturated to the edge of monochrome — neutral greys, dirty bone-white, gunmetal, dark steel — with only two exceptions: the DULL GOLDEN-TAN of the aramid line, and the MUTED BRICK RED of the YGGD marking. Slightly cool, filmic, low saturation, gentle contrast, deep neutral blacks. No teal-and-orange, no warm grade, no filter look.
MAINTAIN
ONE compact hand-sized descent anchor on neutral seamless grey. Minimal machined design, few parts, few seams, no greebles and no screens. Dirty bone-white shell over gunmetal, one crisp shut-line, matte and scuffed. Three short blunt hardened spikes driven out of the recessed underside, worn bright at the tips and packed with pale stone dust. A THIN dull golden-tan aramid line feeding from a slot in one end and lying out in a long relaxed curve, sealed with a dark alloy ferrule. One knurled brake wheel and one recessed stud, nothing else. YGGD etched small in muted brick red on the top face, four letters, spelled correctly, once. 35mm anamorphic, soft raking key, desaturated filmic grade, film grain. No text overlays, no hands, no background, no second object.

A clean PROP REFERENCE PLATE of a single piece of equipment: a coiled descent rope and its hardware, photographed as a production art department reference. This is a still image, not a scene.
WHAT IT IS
A DESCENT ROPE RIG belonging to a used, field-worn science-fiction infantry kit. It is not sports climbing gear and not a decorative prop — it is issued equipment that has been down a lot of holes.
THE ROPE. A static kernmantle line, roughly 11mm, laid in a NEAT FIGURE-OF-EIGHT COIL about forty centimetres across, the coil bound at its waist with two turns of its own tail and a tucked bight. The sheath is DIRTY BONE-WHITE and PALE GREY — the same worn off-white as the exosuit — with ONE MUTED BRICK-RED TRACER THREAD spiralling through the weave. The braid pattern is crisp and visible: tight diagonal chevrons, individual filaments catching light. It is grubby: grey dust ground into the weave, darker soiling where hands and a device have run over it, a few fibres fuzzed proud of the sheath, one small scorched-glossy patch where it ran fast through metal.
THE END. One free end lies out of the coil across the surface, its termination HEAT-SEALED and capped in a machined dark-grey alloy ferrule.
THE HARDWARE. Clipped to the coil, a compact machined DESCENDER — hard anodised gunmetal and dirty bone-white plates, an alloy bobbin, a knurled friction lever, hex fasteners, chamfered edges, small engraved index marks. LOGO LAW
【THE WORD IS Y-G-G-D. FOUR LETTERS. NOTHING ELSE.】
It is spelled correctly and identically in both places. NO other words, NO tagline, NO second brand, NO invented lettering, NO decorative script, NO glow, NO emblem, NO circle around it, NO barcode. It is stamped industrial marking, not a fashion label.
FAIL TEST: IF THE LETTERS ARE MISSPELLED, DUPLICATED, REVERSED OR JOINED INTO NONSENSE, IT IS WRONG.

A macro-lens cinematic film still captures an extreme close-up of a single, very small shoe sized for a young adult lying on its side on a silty, dust-coated floor within the interior of an abandoned school. A close-up, straight-on macro lens shot focuses on a painted chart displaying rows of small, faded handprints on a wall inside a long-abandoned school. An extreme close-up, macro lens shot captures a thickly textured child's finger painting in an abandoned school, with the paint now dried, cracked, and peeling into a mosaic of curling, uneven flakes reminiscent of a long-parched riverbed. A wide-angle, straight-on shot, capturing the monumental scale of a long, abandoned school corridor. A low-angle, wide anamorphic shot captures the textured wall of an abandoned school classroom. An extreme macro close-up shot captures a corroded metal tin of crayons placed on a decrepit wooden desk inside an abandoned schoolroom. Fine photographic grain permeates the image, signaling a high-quality, natural light analog film capture achieved with a macro lens and extremely shallow depth of field—only the crayons and closest rust in sharp focus, while everything beyond and behind rapidly falls away in a creamy blur. A cinematic macro close-up captures an upturned costume box on the dusty concrete floor of a derelict school interior. A wide-angle shot, reminiscent of a cinematic film still, features an immense, long-abandoned concrete courtyard situated at the interior of a derelict school. A low-angle wide shot with strong horizontal anamorphic compression details a deserted school corridor, taken from floor level with the camera nearly flush against the wet linoleum surface. A wide anamorphic film still, low, near-eye-level angle showing a battered ceramic drinking fountain attached to a grime-smeared corridor wall. A wide anamorphic film still frames a view from inside a dark classroom doorway, peering out into the corridor of an abandoned school. A close-up macro lens cinematic film still of a weathered papier-mâché mask hangs from a rusty nail against a cracked wall in an abandoned schoolroom, its faded paint crazed and flaking from decades of neglect. A straight-on, tightly cropped close-up film still shot with a macro lens captures a decorative classroom alphabet frieze in extreme disrepair. An extreme close-up macro shot depicts a weathered, partially torn piece of paper displaying a child's drawing of a house and a sun in the upper corner; the artwork remains partially readable despite heavy age-related damage, with the paper taking on a frayed, fabric-like appearance after centuries of neglect. A dimly lit wide-angle shot, reminiscent of a cinematic film still, frames the abandoned school corridor in an ultra-wide anamorphic aspect ratio. An extreme close-up, macro lens shot in a desaturated teal-green color palette captures a small, weathered wooden name plaque or peg label affixed to a coat rail inside an abandoned school setting.
